summary: All six Expect lines hold at 6d7a6b7. I wrote my own toy tournament (toy/2026-11-04-recipe-cards, six lanes: three pass every floor, and one each fails a scenario, a contract test and a hard constraint) and my own judge file for 2026-11-04-stage-contract round 2 (rescore/judge-round2.json from result2.md, with rescore/scores-round2.json copied from the round-2 measure2.json files). I wrote both before reading the builder's tests. My tests (16) pass. npm test: 546 tests, 534 pass, 1 fail, which is the known environmental copy-not-link release-tags test. Doubts: primitive usage per model stage is a judgement call. My judge counts S 12 (13 weighted) and M 13 (14 weighted), and the builder's judge.json counts 13 and 14 with a different split between counted and special. Either reading gives the same qualified set and the same ranking. score.mjs trusts the judge's stage lists and does not check them against the workflow JSON (a risk the item already names).

P-pass Counted: step-list, source-ref (x2) -> 2 counted (3 weighted). Special cases: fraction-table: used by 2 of 4 model stages; menu-week-grid: used by 1 of 4 model stages ...; used in one workflow (menu); print-css: used by no model stage. Q-lean (stages only in workflow card): step-list: used in one workflow (card) -> special; source-ref with workflows [menu] -> counted; inline-units: 1 of 2 model stages; used in one workflow (card). counted + special equals every primitive listed, so none is dropped.

score.mjs ranks only through dominates(): a lane must be at least as good on every trade-off and better on one, and a missing value blocks a rank. It computes no composite. Toy: Q-lean has fewer primitives (1 vs 3 weighted) but more bytes (200 vs 100), so neither ranks above the other and both are in tier 1. P beats R only because it equals R on primitives and bytes and is better on trials. The Markdown row shows all three: '| P-pass | 2 counted (3 weighted), 3 special | 100 | 1 passed of 1 | R-untried |'.
